title.narrative: An Africa Consortium’s Response to Advancing Women, Peace, and Security (WPS) in Ethiopia (2024-2027): Building Localization and Resilience for the Women's Peace and Security Agenda

description.narrative: To strengthen the localization and resilience of the Women's Peace and Security (WPS) agenda in Ethiopia by empowering local peace leaders and Stakeholders, enhancing institutional capacities of local organisations with strategic thinking, exchange of good regional practices, and technical skills, and by contributing to fostering sustainable and inclusive peace processes that ensure the active meaningful participation and leadership of women in conflict its mitigation, prevention, transformative resolution, and post-conflict recovery over a twenty eight month period.

recipient-country.narrative:
The Ethiopia conflict, particularly the devastating war between the Federal Government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), has plunged the nation into severe turmoil, exacerbating deep-seated ethnic and political tensions. Over the past five years, Ethiopia hasfaced a cascade of conflicts across various regions, rooted in ethnic rivalries, land disputes, and struggles for political power. This instability has severely undermined economic, social, and political structures, leaving lasting scars on the nation's social fabric. The Tigray war, beginning in November 2020, stands out for its extreme human toll, characterized by mass displacement, human rights violations, and widespread sexual violence, disproportionately affecting women and girls. The war has displaced over a million people, with women and children making up more than 70% of those affected, compounding Ethiopia’s already dire humanitarian crisis.
The conflict’s impact extends beyond Tigray to neighboring regions, such as Afar and Amhara, disrupting communities and causing significant psychological trauma. In Tigray, two in five young people face mental health challenges, and countless women, often widowed and stigmatized, struggle to sustain their families. Despite their vital roles in community rebuilding, women continue to be seen largely as victims rather than leaders and peace agents. This marginalization is stark, particularly considering the disproportionate impact of conflict on women and the mandates of UN Security Council Resolution 1325, which emphasizes women's meaningful participation in peace and security efforts.
Despite the resolution’s directives and Ethiopia's historical ties to the WPS agenda, women remain vastly underrepresented in formal peace processes. The African Union-mediated peace deal, brokered after two years of brutal conflict by H.E. Olusegun Obasanjo and other high-level figures, resulted in a cessation of hostilities without significant female involvement—aside from one women on the AU High Level Mediation Panel -Her Excellency Phumzile Mlambo Ngcuka. The exclusion of women in these critical dialogues illustrates the entrenched gender barriers in peace negotiations.
Yet, Ethiopian women have persisted in advancing the Women, Peace, and Security agenda, working tirelessly to implement and popularize UNSCR 1325 and its nine subsequent resolutions. Efforts include linking WPS initiatives to the AU’s FemWise Africa women mediators’ network. Ethiopia has been an early adopter, launching a national FemWise chapter and remaining among the few countries actively integrating this continental initiative. These ongoing efforts highlight the urgent need to bridge the gap between international commitments and on-the-ground realities, ensuring women's leadership in shaping a peaceful, resilient Ethiopia.

condition.narrative: In response to Ethiopia’s urgent need for sustainable peace and stability amid ongoing ethnic and political conflicts, the proposed twenty-eight-month initiative, "An Africa Consortium’s Response to Advancing Women, Peace, and Security (WPS) in Ethiopia (2024-2027)," aims to strengthen the localization and resilience of the Women, Peace, and Security (WPS) agenda in Ethiopia. Led by a strategic consortium comprising The African Centre for the Constructive Resolution of Disputes (ACCORD), the Network of Ethiopian Women’s Associations (NEWA), and the African Women Peace and Security Institute (AWPSI), this project seeks to empower local actors, enhance local institutional capacities, and aims to contribute to strengthening the roles of Ethiopian women as leaders, negotiators and peacebuilders in the prevention, and resolution a conflict and in post-conflict recovery. Building on existing governmental, and civil society efforts, as well as a variety of stakeholders committed to the WPS Agenda, the initiative will support the Ethiopian government’s ongoing policy revisions and development, including the development of a new gender policy and the country’s first National Action Plan (NAP) on WPS, spearheaded by the Ministry of Women and Social Affairs. The project will actively engage with the National Dialogue Commission (NDC), which is tasked with fostering national reconciliation but has faced challenges in ensuring women’s meaningful representation. By advocating for more inclusive and gender-responsive dialogue mechanisms, the initiative aims to strengthen women's roles in key decision-making processes. It will also work alongside the African Union-led peace negotiations, and other peace efforts in addressing the gaps in women and youths meaningful participation and amplifying women’s agency, voices and power to engage in decision making and contributing in high-level peace talks. The project will harness civil society's crucial role by collaborating with networks such as Ethiopian Women Peacebuilders (EWPB), which empowers women leaders across regions to engage in peacebuilding activities. It will through the consortium partner NEWA support TIMRAN’s coalition of 27 CSOs advocating for women's inclusion in the national dialogue and work with the Ethiopian Peace Institute’s CSO Coalition to monitor and sustain WPS commitments. Additionally, the initiative will leverage the Presidential Leadership Program, launched by former President Sahle-Work Zewde, to provide WPS-focused leadership training, thereby enhancing women’s influence in peace and security sectors at both federal and regional levels. This comprehensive approach envisions contributing to building the foundations of a future where women are central to Ethiopia's sustainable, inclusive peace processes, with tangible impact in conflict mitigation, transformative resolution, and recovery efforts.
